extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and practitioners interested in U.S. environmental and administrative law and Supreme Court decisions
extracted.subtask_short: EPA authority under Clean Air Act §111(d)
extracted.subtask_description: Explanatory summary of the legal standards, doctrines, and procedural history governing the EPA's authority to regulate greenhouse gas emissions from existing power plants under Clean Air Act §111(d), as addressed in West Virginia v. EPA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 7411(d) authority: 'best system of emission reduction'
rubrics_metrics.description: As part of the amended Clean Air Act, under § 7411(d) Congress granted the EPA authority to identify the 'best system of emission reduction' from power generating plants or other large stationary sources, and work with states to complete implementation plans to incorporate those systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This authority is split between § 7411(b) for new plants and § 7411(d) for existing plants. Within § 7411(d) the EPA cannot set taxes or fines on plants that fail to meet emission standards, but it can work with states in implementation plans to require installation of emissions-control technology, participate in emissions-trading programs, or allow states to implement their own taxes on violating plants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Within-the-fenceline vs outside-the-fenceline limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Clean Power Plan distinguished between regulation 'within the fence line' (emissions-reduction technology at individual plants) and 'outside the fence line' (generation shifting to alternative clean energy sources such as solar and wind).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opponents argued the EPA overreached by using § 7411(d) to require actions 'outside the fence line' such as efficiency improvements and renewable generation; the Court's decision emphasized limits on using § 7411(d) to mandate generation shifting beyond plant-level controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Michigan v. EPA — requirement to consider costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Michigan v. EPA, the EPA must consider costs when issuing a 'finding' that it is 'necessary and appropriate' to regulate; the Court held the agency acted unreasonably when it determined it did not need to consider costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This standard requires cost assessment as part of the agency's decision-making process and has been criticized for potentially minimizing health impacts; it influences what technologies or standards the EPA may adopt because costs may limit feasible options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major questions doctrine — clear congressional authorization for extraordinary agency action
rubrics_metrics.description: When a proposed agency action falls under the 'major questions doctrine', courts require the agency to point to 'clear congressional authorization' for the power it claims, beyond a merely plausible textual basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Roberts wrote that 'certain extraordinary cases... make us 'reluctant to read into ambiguous statutory text' the delegation claimed to be lurking there.' Agencies therefore must identify explicit statutory text or legislative history that clearly authorizes sweeping regulatory programs (the Court applied this doctrine to the CPP).

rubrics_metrics.name: Chevron deference and its limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Chevron v. NRDC established that courts often defer to reasonable agency interpretations of ambiguous statutes. West Virginia v. EPA invoked doctrines (like major questions) that limit such deference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes that the West Virginia decision 'did not go as far' as removing Chevron entirely, but later cases (Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, 2024) overruled Chevron; the evolving status of Chevron affects how courts review agency statutory interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arbitrary-and-capricious standard (APA) in rulemaking review
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may vacate agency rules under the Administrative Procedure Act if rulemaking is 'arbitrary and capricious' or based on a fundamental misconstruction of the statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The D.C. Circuit vacated the Affordable Clean Energy (ACE) rule as arbitrary and capricious, finding its implementation 'hinged on a fundamental misconstruction' of § 7411(d). This demonstrates that statutory interpretation errors or inadequate reasoning can invalidate agency rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mootness and stays: 'absolutely clear' standard for mootness; use of stays to prevent irreversible compliance costs
rubrics_metrics.description: A case is not moot unless it is 'absolutely clear that the allegedly wrongful behavior could not reasonably be expected to recur.' The Supreme Court may issue stays to prevent parties from incurring irreversible compliance costs while litigation proceeds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Roberts rejected the EPA's mootness argument for the CPP under this standard. The Court previously issued an unsigned stay in February 2016 to halt CPP implementation—motivated in part by concern companies would spend money to comply before final resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nondelegation doctrine concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: The litigation raised concerns that expansive agency rulemaking might implicate the nondelegation doctrine — whether Congress has unconstitutionally delegated legislative power to the executive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observers noted the case could lead courts to scrutinize whether Congress provided sufficiently clear standards when delegating authority to agencies; major-questions analysis can intersect with nondelegation arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative amendment can supply clear authorization (role of Congress)
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress can amend statutes to explicitly grant agencies the authorities courts find lacking; following the decision, the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) amended the Clean Air Act to designate greenhouse gases as air pollutants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The IRA's explicit language was described as addressing major-questions concerns by codifying Massachusetts v. EPA and providing clearer congressional authorization for regulating greenhouse gases. Legal experts debate whether such amendments fully cover actions like generation shifting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on EPA enforcement mechanisms under § 7411(d)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under § 7411(d) the EPA cannot itself set taxes or fines on plants failing to meet standards but may require technology installation, allow emissions trading, or permit states to impose taxes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Additionally, actions that cause a plant to be subject to New Source Review (e.g., significant efficiency upgrades) can have regulatory consequences; agencies must consider such statutory interactions when designing rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial use of the 'shadow docket' / emergency procedural posture
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court's use of emergency orders and stays (the 'shadow docket') featured prominently in the CPP litigation, including stays issued before lower-court resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes this was among the first high-profile uses of the shadow docket to halt agency action, and commentators debated its appropriateness and impact on administrative and regulatory processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical infrequency of using § 7411(d) increases judicial scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: The EPA had rarely invoked § 7411(d) in rule-making, meaning that § 7411(d) historically received less legal scrutiny than other parts of the Clean Air Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The relative novelty of invoking § 7411(d) for broad, economy-wide measures (like generation shifting) contributed to judicial and political contestation; novel statutory uses tend to invite more intensive judicial review and doctrinal scrutiny.
